topicName: Memory Management, Eviction Policies, and maxmemory
content: [{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Mastering Memory Management, Eviction Policies, and maxmemory in Redis"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Redis is an in-memory data store, which makes it exceptionally fast. However, physical RAM is finite. Without proper memory management, Redis can consume all available system memory, leading to out-of-memory (OOM) crashes, swap thrashing, or forced termination by the operating system kernel. This tutorial explores how Redis manages memory, how to configure limits using maxmemory, and how eviction policies protect your infrastructure."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Understanding maxmemory"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"The maxmemory directive in the redis.conf configuration file dictates the maximum amount of memory Redis can consume. Once this limit is reached, Redis reacts based on the configured eviction policy. You can configure maxmemory in bytes, or using human-readable suffixes like megabytes (mb), gigabytes (gb), etc."},{"order":5,"type":"code","text":"maxmemory 2gb"},{"order":6,"type":"paragraph","text":"You can also configure maxmemory dynamically at runtime using the Redis CLI CONFIG SET command without requiring a service restart:"},{"order":7,"type":"code","text":"CONFIG SET maxmemory 2147483648"},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"How Redis Calculates Memory Usage"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"When maxmemory is evaluated, Redis looks at its internal memory consumption (visible via the INFO memory command under used_memory). This includes:"},{"order":10,"type":"bullet_point","text":"The memory used by user keys and their respective values."},{"order":11,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Internal overheads, such as the pointer structures and dictionaries used to store keys."},{"order":12,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Client output buffers, replication buffers, and Lua script memory."},{"order":13,"type":"subheading","text":"Redis Eviction Policies"},{"order":14,"type":"paragraph","text":"When memory reaches the maxmemory threshold and Redis needs to allocate space for new writes, it selects keys to remove based on the maxmemory-policy. If no policy is set, write commands that require additional memory will fail with an error."},{"order":15,"type":"bullet_point","text":"noeviction: Returns an error when memory limit is reached and a write command is attempted (default for older versions)."},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"allkeys-lru: Evicts the least recently used (LRU) keys across all keys, making space for new data."},{"order":17,"type":"bullet_point","text":"volatile-lru: Evicts the least recently used (LRU) keys, but only among keys that have an expiration set (TTL)."},{"order":18,"type":"bullet_point","text":"allkeys-random: Randomly evicts keys across all keys to free up memory."},{"order":19,"type":"bullet_point","text":"volatile-random: Randomly evicts keys that have an expiration set."},{"order":20,"type":"bullet_point","text":"volatile-ttl: Evicts keys with the shortest time-to-live (TTL) remaining, restricted to keys with an expiration."},{"order":21,"type":"bullet_point","text":"allkeys-lfu: Evicts the least frequently used (LFU) keys across all keys."},{"order":22,"type":"bullet_point","text":"volatile-lfu: Evicts the least frequently used (LFU) keys among keys with an expiration set."},{"order":23,"type":"subheading","text":"Configuring Eviction Policies"},{"order":24,"type":"paragraph","text":"You can define the eviction policy inside redis.conf or update it dynamically via the Redis CLI."},{"order":25,"type":"code","text":"maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru"},{"order":26,"type":"paragraph","text":"Runtime adjustment via CONFIG SET:"},{"order":27,"type":"code","text":"CONFIG SET maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru"},{"order":28,"type":"subheading","text":"Best Practices for Production Environments"},{"order":29,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Leave headroom: Never set maxmemory to 100% of physical RAM. Leave at least 20-30 percent headroom for OS operations, forks during snapshotting (RDB/AOF), and memory fragmentation."},{"order":30,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Choose LRU vs LFU: Use LFU (Least Frequently Used) if you have skewed workloads where some keys are accessed heavily regardless of how recently they were touched. Use LRU for standard temporal locality patterns."},{"order":31,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Monitor Memory Metrics: Frequently check memory fragmentation ratio and used memory via 'INFO memory' to tune your infrastructure effectively."}]
